title: State v. Mara Voss
teaser: A violin worth $1.2 million leaves a locked vault during a sold-out recital. The young woman who restored it says she had gone home.
summary: The Calloway violin, made in 1714 and insured for $1.2 million, vanished from the vault at Aldgate Conservatory during a recital on the evening of March 9. Its owner, the collector Lucian Hargrave, found the vault empty at 9:40 PM. Mara Voss, 27, an apprentice luthier who had spent six weeks restoring the instrument, was arrested two days later. She says she never went near the vault that night.

evidence.label: The vault keypad
evidence.detail: Voss's personal code opened the vault at 7:26 PM. The codes were written on a card taped inside the workshop cabinet, and three staff admit they had seen it.

evidence.label: The car park barrier
evidence.detail: Voss told police she left at 6:15 PM. The barrier recorded her car leaving at 7:41 PM. Confronted, she said she had stayed to finish a repair and got the time wrong.

evidence.label: Her debts
evidence.detail: Voss owed $84,000 for her mother's care home and was three months behind. She had kept up partial payments every month from an apprentice's wage.

evidence.label: The Geneva email
evidence.detail: Eleven days before the theft, Voss emailed a Geneva dealer asking what a Calloway-school violin might fetch. She used her conservatory address and says a private client asked her to find out.

evidence.label: The varnish
evidence.detail: Traces of the violin's rare amber varnish were found on the cuff of Voss's coat. She had worked on that violin most days for six weeks.

evidence.label: The empty case
evidence.detail: The violin's case turned up, wiped clean, in a bin behind Voss's building on March 11. That bin serves forty flats and backs onto an open alley.

evidence.label: The insurance rider
evidence.detail: Five weeks before the theft, Hargrave raised the violin's cover from $800,000 to $1.2 million. Accounts show his firm lost money for two years running.

evidence.label: The corridor camera
evidence.detail: The camera outside the vault was off for maintenance from 7 PM to 8 PM. The booking was made by Hargrave's assistant three days earlier.

witnesses.name: Bram Hollis
witnesses.statement: Saw a woman in a dark coat near the vault stairs at about 7:30, carrying something long. The stairs are lit only by exit signs, and he never saw her face. He says she walked like Mara.

witnesses.name: Cecily Rowe
witnesses.statement: Booked the camera maintenance and calls it routine. Agreed under cross-examination that it was the first such booking she had ever made, and that Mr Hargrave had reminded her to do it.

witnesses.name: Det. Anton Pike
witnesses.statement: Searched Voss's flat, workshop and accounts and found no violin, no buyer and no money. Agreed that he never looked at Hargrave's finances until the defence asked.

witnesses.name: Yusuf Demir
witnesses.statement: Received Voss's email and thought nothing of it. Says a man who wouldn't give his name telephoned a week later asking the same question.

points.claim: Her own code opened the vault during the recital
She lied to police about when she left
Her car left 15 minutes after the vault was opened
She owed $84,000 and was three months behind
She priced this kind of violin eleven days before it vanished
The violin's varnish was on her coat
The empty case was dumped behind her building
The caretaker knew her walk at the vault stairs
People that deep in debt will take whatever they can reach
The codes were on a card that three staff had seen
Nobody robs a vault using their own personal code
Six weeks on that violin explains the varnish
Hargrave raised the insurance by $400,000 five weeks before
Hargrave's firm was losing money and he had the motive
Hargrave's own assistant switched off the camera for that exact hour
She had never booked maintenance before, and Hargrave reminded her to
No violin, no buyer and no money were ever found

fixations.2: Whoever spoke last and sounded sure.
fixations.3: She lied to the police about when she left. People who've done nothing don't lie.
fixations.4: The insurance rider and the keypad log. Those are numbers, and numbers can be priced.
fixations.5: What debt like that does to a person. You've seen families choose between rent and medicine.
fixations.6: Whether a caretaker can really know someone's walk in the dark.
fixations.8: The hour the camera went dark, and who arranged it.
fixations.9: A woman who spends six weeks caring for an instrument, and what it would take to sell it.
fixations.10: Her debts. In your experience people who can't pay always find a way to take.
fixations.11: A search that began and ended with the apprentice, and never reached the rich man.

record.reason: Her code opened the vault, she was in the building when it opened, and she lied about that to the police. She had a debt she couldn't pay and had asked what such a violin was worth. Hargrave's insurance and the dark camera raise real questions, but none of it explains why an innocent person gives a false time. On what was presented, the case against her holds, narrowly.

beats: Mara Voss did not take the violin. She never opened the vault.
Lucian Hargrave sold it in January, privately, to a buyer in another country. He still needed it to be stolen.
The client who asked Mara to price a Calloway-school violin worked for him. So did the man who rang Geneva, checking that the email had arrived.
The card in the workshop cabinet told him her code. Cecily Rowe booked the camera because she was told to, and she never asked why.
Mara lied about 7:41 because she had been in the workshop doing paid repairs on the side, which would have ended her apprenticeship. It was how she paid the care home.
The varnish was six weeks of honest work. Even the bin was chosen.
He collected $1.2 million. He sent flowers to the conservatory.
truth.closing: A clean case isn't the same thing as a true one. Sometimes it's clean because someone took great care.
